newsitem.title: USA: N.Y.C. hopes court will let it sell water system.
newsitem.headline: N.Y.C. hopes court will let it sell water system.

text.p: New York City, which lost the first two rounds of a court fight to sell its water and sewer system, on Thursday said it hoped the state's highest court will agree to let the sale to go forward this spring.

"It is possible, but again not certain, that title transfer would begin to take place next spring," said Mark Page, executive director of the Municipal Water Finance Authority, at a conference held by the utility.

He explained that the city recently won the Court of Appeal's agreement to issue an expedited decision, which means that the case likely will be argued in February and a decision handed down as soon as March.

The sale has been opposed by the city comptroller, Alan Hevesi, who said he would not approve having the Water Authority issue approximately $2.3 billion in bonds to buy the system over four years. About $1.3 billion of the bonds would be used to retire outstanding issues.

The Water Authority official argued that its recent purchase of a private water system in Jamaica sets a precedent for its court fight with the comptroller. Hevesi also has argued that the utility lacked the broad statutory authority needed to buy New York City's water and sewer system.

For its capital plan for the year ending June 30, New York City is considering including the proceeds of a little under $2 billion of debt to retire the $1.3 billion of outstanding issues and pay the first installment on the purchase. That installment totals about $600 million.
"It is possible that the Water Authority would be doing certainly not an all-in-one bond sale, but several bond sales next spring to accommodate that additional capital need," said Page.
The price the Authority would pay for the system as the new bonds are repaid over 30 years will amount to less than the utility can be expected to pay the city in its long-term lease, Page said.

"We believe that the $2.3 billion purchase price basically can be paid for at less than what we think is a pretty conservative estimate, that is a low estimate of what the annual lease payment would be for the next 30 years."
The lease runs for 40 years from 1985 or as long as the the Agency has water debt outstanding.

The Giuliani Administration also is considering whether to propose an alternative transaction to the sale, which would involve the $1.3 billion refunding, according to the sale documents for the utility's $371 million bond sale in October.
The city official, who said there would not be a significant impact on the authority's revenues from its water conservation efforts, added that the outlook for rates was quite moderate.
